did_you_know.text: In the ancient world, changing clothes could symbolize purification or preparation for worship. That is why Jacob connects it with removing the foreign gods.
The elah was a large tree common in the Land of Israel, probably a terebinth rather than an ordinary oak. Such trees could also serve as landmarks and burial places.
The expression “terror of God” means an extraordinary fear believed to have been caused by God. Because of this fear, the surrounding cities did not pursue Jacob’s family.
Luz was the place’s earlier name, while Bethel means “house of God.” The two names are mentioned together to connect the old place with its new meaning.
Deborah was Rebekah’s nurse, so she had probably accompanied the family for many years. Rebekah is not mentioned here, but Deborah’s death receives special attention.
A libation was a liquid poured as part of a religious ritual, and oil was also used in the ancient Near East to mark dedication. Jacob thus shows that the place is sacred and personally significant.
The word “kivrat” is an ancient measure whose exact meaning is uncertain, so translations suggest different distances. Ephrath is identified later in the chapter with Bethlehem.

Rachel named her son Ben-Oni, a name usually connected with her sorrow, while Jacob called him Benjamin. Benjamin is generally understood as “son of the right hand” or “son of strength,” expressing hope rather than only pain.
Jacob’s twelve sons become the basis for lists of the twelve tribes of Israel. In later lists, Joseph is sometimes represented through his two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh.
Isaac lived for 180 years—longer than Abraham, who lived 175 years, and Jacob, who lived 147 years. Thus Isaac had the longest lifespan of the three patriarchs.
